nota.t: Types of variation

t: Direct: y = kx; inverse: y = k/x; joint: y = kx/z.
Find k from one pair of values, then substitute.

nota.t: 1.3 Joint Variation

Combined variation joins direct and/or inverse variation. Joint variation: y ∝ xz means y varies directly as the product of x and z. Combined with inverse: y ∝ x/z. For example, the volume of a gas varies directly as temperature and inversely as pressure.

t: y ∝ xz ⇒ y = kxz
y ∝ x/z ⇒ y = kx/z
find k once, then use it for new values

nota.t:
Example: P ∝ Q/R², P = 3 when Q = 12, R = 2.
3 = k(12)/4 → k = 1. When Q = 18, R = 3: P = 18/9 = 2.
1.2 Inverse Variation

Inverse variation happens when one quantity increases and the other decreases in proportion. If y varies inversely as x, y ∝ 1/x, then y = k/x or xy = k. For example, travel time varies inversely as speed. The graph of y against x is a hyperbola that never touches the axes.

t: y ∝ 1/xⁿ ⇔ y = k/xⁿ
x₁ⁿy₁ = x₂ⁿy₂
Example: number of workers and time to finish a job

nota.t:
Example: y ∝ 1/x, y = 6 when x = 4.
k = xy = 24, so y = 24/x.
When x = 8: y = 3.

v.c: Inverse variation graph: y falls as x grows

nota.t: 1.1 Direct Variation

Direct variation happens when one quantity increases and another increases at the same rate. If y varies directly as x, written y ∝ x, then y = kx where k is the constant of variation. The graph of y against x is a straight line through the origin. It can also involve powers, such as y ∝ x² or y ∝ √x.

t: y ∝ xⁿ ⇔ y = kxⁿ
k = y ÷ xⁿ (found from one pair of values)
y₁/x₁ⁿ = y₂/x₂ⁿ
Write the relation: y = kxⁿ
Substitute the given values to find k
Write the full equation
Substitute to find the required value

nota.t:
Example: y ∝ x², y = 18 when x = 3.
18 = k(3²) → k = 2, so y = 2x².
When x = 5: y = 2(25) = 50.

v.c: Direct variation graph: a straight line through the origin

nota.t: 2 × 2 matrices

t: Determinant ad − bc; inverse = 1/(ad − bc) [d −b; −c a].
Simultaneous equations: AX = B → X = A⁻¹B.

nota.t: 2.1 Matrices

A matrix is an arrangement of numbers in rows and columns inside brackets. Its order is m × n (m rows, n columns). Element aᵢⱼ is in row i, column j. Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and corresponding elements are equal. Matrices store data such as sales or marks.

t: Square matrix: m = n
Zero matrix O: all elements 0
Identity matrix I: 1s on the main diagonal

nota.t: 2.2 Basic Operations on Matrices

Matrices of the same order can be added or subtracted element by element. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by a number. A (m × n) and B (n × p) can be multiplied if A's columns equal B's rows; the result is m × p, each element = row × column. In general AB ≠ BA. The inverse A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹ = I and solves simultaneous linear equations.

t: A = [a b; c d] ⇒ A⁻¹ = 1/(ad − bc) [d −b; −c a]
ad − bc = 0 ⇒ no inverse
Equation AX = B ⇒ X = A⁻¹B
Write the simultaneous equations as AX = B
Find the determinant ad − bc
Find A⁻¹
Multiply: X = A⁻¹B

nota.t: Insurance

t: Premium = (face value ÷ 1000) × rate.
Co-insurance: compensation = (bought ÷ required) × loss − deductible.

nota.t: 3.1 Risk and Insurance Coverage

Risk is the chance of a loss. Insurance moves risk from a person to an insurer in return for a premium. Life insurance covers a life; general insurance covers property (motor, fire, travel, medical). Key terms: policy, premium, deductible (the amount you pay yourself) and co-insurance (sharing the loss).

t: Premium = (sum insured ÷ 1 000) × premium rate
Co-insurance: required insurance = co-insurance % × property value
Payout = (insured ÷ required) × loss − deductible

nota.t:
Example: house RM400 000, 80% co-insurance, insured RM240 000, loss RM50 000, deductible RM2 000.
Required = 0.8 × 400 000 = RM320 000.
Payout = (240 000 ÷ 320 000) × 50 000 − 2 000 = RM35 500.
Tax

t: Chargeable income = income − exemptions − reliefs.
Rebates come off the tax.

nota.t: 4.1 Taxation

Tax is a compulsory payment to the government to fund development and public services. Direct tax is charged on people or companies (income tax, property tax); indirect tax is charged on goods and services (sales and service tax, import duty). Income tax is worked out from chargeable income after exemptions and reliefs, then rebates are subtracted.

t: Chargeable income = total income − exemptions − reliefs
Tax uses progressive rates
Tax payable = tax − rebates − monthly deductions (PCB)

nota.t:
Example: annual income RM60 000, reliefs RM17 000 → chargeable income RM43 000.
Tax = RM600 (on the first RM35 000) + 8% × 8 000 = RM600 + RM640 = RM1 240.

v.c: Steps to work out income tax

nota.t: Enlargement

t: Image side = |k| × object side; image area = k² × object area.

nota.t: 5.1 Congruency

Two shapes are congruent if they have the same shape and size. Congruent triangles are proved with SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA, AAS or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, side). Translations, reflections and rotations give images congruent to the object.

t: AAA does not prove congruence (only similarity)
Corresponding sides and angles are equal

v.l: congruent: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS

nota.t: 5.3 Combined Transformations

A combined transformation means doing two or more transformations in turn. AB means B is done first, then A. Two translations combine into one translation; two reflections in parallel lines equal a translation; two reflections in intersecting lines equal a rotation.

t: Order matters: AB ≠ BA in general
Equivalent transformation: one single transformation giving the same image

v.c: Combined transformation AB: B first, then A

nota.t: 5.2 Enlargement

An enlargement changes the size of an object from a centre of enlargement with scale factor k. k = image distance from the centre ÷ object distance from the centre. If k > 1 the image is larger; 0 < k < 1 smaller; negative k puts the image on the opposite side, inverted. Area of image = k² × area of object.

t: Draw lines from the centre through each vertex
Measure each distance and multiply by k
Mark the image vertices and join them

nota.t: Example: object area 6 cm², k = 3 → image area = 3² × 6 = 54 cm².

topik.nama: 6. Ratios and Graphs of Trigonometric Functions

nota.t: Graphs

t: y = a sin bx + c: amplitude |a|, period 360°/b, max a + c, min c − a.
All-Sin-Tan-Cos for quadrants I–IV.

nota.t: 6.2 Graphs of Sine, Cosine and Tangent

The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x are waves repeating every 360° with maximum 1 and minimum −1. y = tan x repeats every 180° with asymptotes at x = 90° and 270°. For y = a sin bx + c: a changes the amplitude, b the number of cycles in 360°, and c shifts the graph up or down.

t: Amplitude = |a|
Period = 360° ÷ b
sin and cos: range −1 to 1

nota.t: 6.1 Sine, Cosine and Tangent of 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°

The unit circle gives trigonometric ratios for any angle 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°. For a point (x, y) on it, cos θ = x, sin θ = y and tan θ = y/x. Signs depend on the quadrant: I all positive, II sin positive, III tan positive, IV cos positive. The reference angle is the acute angle with the x-axis.

t: Find the quadrant of the angle
Find the reference angle
Find the ratio for the reference angle
Give it the sign for that quadrant

nota.t:
Example: cos 240°. Quadrant III, reference angle 240° − 180° = 60°.
cos 60° = 0.5, cos is negative in quadrant III → cos 240° = −0.5.

v.c: A 150° angle on the unit circle

topik.nama: 7. Measures of Dispersion for Grouped Data

nota.t: Grouped data

t: Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf (midpoints).
Interquartile range = Q3 − Q1 from the ogive.

nota.t: 7.1 Dispersion

Dispersion measures how spread out data are from the centre. Grouped data are arranged in class intervals with frequencies. Histograms, frequency polygons and ogives (cumulative frequency graphs) show the spread. Two data sets can share a mean but differ in spread.

t: Find the lower and upper boundaries of each class
Work out cumulative frequencies
Plot cumulative frequency against the upper boundaries
Draw a smooth curve (the ogive)

nota.t: 7.2 Measures of Dispersion

Measures of dispersion for grouped data include the range (highest class midpoint − lowest class midpoint), interquartile range (Q₃ − Q₁, read from the ogive), variance and standard deviation. A small standard deviation means the data are more consistent and close to the mean.

t: Mean x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf
Variance σ² = Σfx² ÷ Σf − x̄²
σ = √variance
Q₁ at position ¼Σf, Q₃ at ¾Σf

v.c: Standard deviation shows the spread around the mean

nota.t: Modelling

t: Identify → assume → build → solve → verify → refine → report.
Linear y = mx + c; exponential P = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ.

nota.t: 8.1 Mathematical Modeling

Mathematical modelling uses mathematics to represent and solve real-world problems. A model may be a linear, quadratic, exponential or variation function. The process repeats: if the model is not good enough, the assumptions and model are refined.
Example: a water bill is RM5 + RM0.57 per m³. Model: C = 5 + 0.57V. For 30 m³, C = 5 + 17.10 = RM22.10.
